A letter from the mayor of Louisville and the president of the University of Louisville:

Moving the Confederate Monument: Why The Time Has Come

By: Greg Fischer, Mayor of Louisville, and James R. Ramsey, President of the University of Louisville

Friends,

This morning we announced the immediate removal of the Confederate Monument located on the University of Louisville’s Belknap Campus, where it has resided on a median on Third Street for over 120 years. The statue will be stored until our offices find an appropriate historical venue to commemorate Kentucky’s unique role in the Civil War, which included soldiers who fought and died for both the Union and Confederacy.

In 1895, the statue was placed in a secluded park-like area of town by the Kentucky Woman’s Monument Association to honor the Kentuckians who fought and died for the Confederacy. We are not removing the statue to erase our state’s history of having soldiers who fought for the South, but we do believe there is a better venue for it than a modern college campus that strives to foster a culture of inclusion for all students, faculty, and staff. The Civil War and history of supporting the Confederacy is in our past, while UofL and its diverse campus full of bright, talented scholars and researchers is our future.

Together, we decided the time had come for the statue’s relocation, a move many in our community believe will continue our march toward greater racial harmony for Louisville. We realize that decisions like this will spark community debate from people who support and oppose such a move, but as leaders chosen to make tough decisions we mutually believe the time has come for this monument to leave campus for a more historically suitable home.

The statue was placed during a time that was much different than ours. There were no automobiles whizzing past a growing and dynamic metropolitan research university. Indeed, when the statue was placed, the area around it was an orphanage in a park-like setting.

Over time, the statue has been a source of controversy for citizens and students alike. The University of Louisville campus has grown to encircle the monument, and it does not symbolize the values of the city of Louisville and our diverse campus community.

Since Dr. Ramsey arrived to the University of Louisville in 2002, the area surrounding the statue has become a bustling thoroughfare used by thousands of people every day. That area has become a home to more than 22,000 undergraduate and graduate students from many racial, religious and socio-economic backgrounds. The university’s Belknap Campus has exploded with new buildings, programs, and economic development installations that benefit our entire region.

Members of the University of Louisville Diversity Committee, composed of students, faculty and staff representatives appointed by President Ramsey, listed the removal of the statue as one of their highest priorities to further foster a culture of diversity and inclusion. We agree with their assessment, and that’s why we took the action we did today. Ultimately, the community of voices on and off campus asking for the statue’s removal proved powerfully persuasive to both of us.

The city of Louisville and the University of Louisville are two of the most inclusive communities in the Commonwealth of Kentucky – a record of which we are incredibly proud. We will continue to examine ways in our respective capacities as Mayor and President to promote inclusivity even as we respect our state’s history.

Once the statue is removed, the median on Third Street will be replaced with a new lane to improve access to the Speed Art Museum and assist traffic flow around the university. Symbolism aside, traffic flow and safety will be drastically improved because of this action.

Let us be clear: we are not attempting to erase our history or dishonor the past sacrifice of any soldier. We simply want to find a better home for the monument—which has fallen into disrepair in its current location—as we respect the wishes of our campus and community at large.

And another letter from the Vice Provost for Diversity and International Affairs at the University of Louisville

Dear Members of the University Community,

Today was a defining moment for the University of Louisville and City of Louisville. I applaud President Ramsey and Mayor Fischer for coming together to begin the immediate removal of the Confederate statue. This is a profound example that exhibits their leadership and commitment to diversity and social justice.

Beginning in the 1980s, if not earlier, UofL students, faculty and staff have called for the statue to be removed. Protests have been held and letters from faculty have been written that provided all of the reasons why the statue should be removed. Similarly, there are community leaders, elected officials and residents who also wanted to see it removed. So to all of the sung and unsung she/heroes from the past and the present who boldly called for the statue to be removed, I want to acknowledge your contributions and say thank you.

We know that the removal of the statue will not erase the vestiges of inequality and injustices, so we must continue to be advocates and activists for social justice.

However nothing should overshadow the importance of this day. It is a win for all of us.

Mordean Taylor-Archer, PhD

Vice Provost for Diversity and International Affairs
